accuracy.evidence: Checked against the National Curriculum in England Year 4 multiplication and division statutory requirement (recognise and use factor pairs and commutativity in mental calculations) and its non-statutory guidance example 2 × 6 × 5 = 10 × 6, and the NCETM Year 4 ready-to-progress guidance (4NF-2/4NF-3: factor pairs, using known facts and the commutative and associative laws mentally). Every product in the lab and items was recomputed: 4 × 15 = 60 in each split, the four factor pairs of 24, 5 × 7 × 2 = 70 in every order, 5 × 18 = 90, 25 × 12 = 300, 5 × 14 = 70, 16 × 5 = 8 × 10 = 80, 15 × 6 = 90 and 16 × 10 = 160 for the slips. The adult text separates commutativity from associativity and states that division and subtraction are not commutative.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets documented multiplicative-reasoning slips (NCETM Year 4 guidance; Anghileri, Teaching Number Sense; Askew on mental strategies): splitting a factor additively, 4 × 5 + 3 (step 1 prediction, challenge 'add', p3); a 'factor pair' that adds rather than multiplies, 5 and 19 (challenge 'sum', p1); counting 6 × 4 as a new pair (step 2 prediction, challenge 'dup', p5); forgetting 1 × n (challenge 'one', m7); believing order changes the product (step 3 prediction, 'order', m1); swapping a division (challenge 'div', m4); and adjusting by moving 1 as in addition, 16 × 5 = 15 × 6 (step 5 prediction, 'comp', m5).

lab_distinct.evidence: flagfsplit is about using factor pairs inside a calculation: a 4 by 15 dot array whose columns are cut into equal groups (red leftover columns when the size is not a factor, 3 blocks of 20 when it is 5), a 1 to 24 number line where each tested factor draws an arc to its partner until the arcs meet in the middle, three swappable cards with a 'do this pair first' box, a friendly-split picker that judges whether the split makes 10 or 100, and a halve-and-double array that re-stacks 16 × 5 into 8 × 10. flagfpair builds tile rectangles to list factors and primes; flagcommul flips one array to show a × b = b × a. Neither computes a product by regrouping. lab_distinct gate passes under 30%.

lab_teaches.evidence: The learner sees each shortcut work before the text names it: groups of 4 leave 3 red columns, groups of 5 give three blocks of 20; testing 5 gives a remainder and testing 6 lands back on 4 × 6, so the arcs stop; swapping cards keeps 70 while the boxed pair changes from 35 to 10; a split that is true but not friendly is accepted as true and the learner is asked for one that makes 10 or 100; halving the columns doubles the rows with the same dot count.

predictions.evidence: Four predictions, each with a tempting wrong option the lab disproves: '4 × 5 + 3' for 4 × 15 (the array shows 20 × 3 = 60), 'Yes, it is a new pair' for 6 × 4 (the arc lands on 4 × 6 again), 'it gets bigger' when the order changes (70 stays 70), and '8 × 10 is bigger' or 'take 8 off both' for 16 × 5 (the re-stacked array still has 80 dots).

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six challenge questions with nine distinct feedback messages naming the slip: adding instead of multiplying the split, a split that does not multiply back, an adding factor pair, counting a turned-round pair twice, forgetting 1 × 24, thinking order matters, swapping a division, moving 1 between factors, and doubling without halving. Answer order rotates between questions.

readability.evidence: Kid text uses short sentences and defines factor pair and commutative in plain words with a worked example each; adult text names the Year 4 statutory wording and the key vocabulary. Canvas labels are short sums or a few words (Do this pair first, They met in the middle). validate_lessons readability passes for kid and adult text.

no_filler.evidence: Filler gate clean. Each kid paragraph carries one idea (finding all factor pairs, commutativity, splitting a factor, making 10 or 100 and halving and doubling). Items mix reasoning types: identifying a factor pair (p1), reorder to make 10 (p2) or 100 (p4, m3), recognising an equivalent split (p3), counting pairs (p5), defining commutative (m1), choosing a strategy (m2, m8), division not commuting (m4), halving and doubling (m5), split then multiply (m6) and the missing 1 × n pair (m7).

mobile.evidence: Checked iPhone 13 light and 360 px Android dark and light screenshots of every step, at the start and after Show me. The 15-column array fits 360 px with 8 px gaps between groups; the number line labels thin to 1 to 8 and multiples of 4 on phones so two-digit numbers never overlap; cards and split chips are 60 px or more; the finished best-split step lists all three worked sums; buttons are full-size lbtn (44 px+). Chips are white with dark ink on both themes.

accessibility.evidence: Every drag or tap has a labelled button twin: Groups of 3, 4 and 5 for the array; Try n for the number line; Swap 1st and 2nd, 2nd and 3rd, 1st and 3rd for the cards; one button per split; Halve and double and Undo. The canvas aria-label is rewritten with each result (leftover columns or the worked 20 × 3, whether n is a factor of 24 and its partner, the bracketed sum after each swap, why a split is true but not friendly, the new array size). walk.cjs axe WCAG 2.1 AA clean in both themes on desktop and iPhone 13.
